Issued at 254 PM EST Tue Nov 24 2026

Rest of Today-Tonight... Upper level trough across the central US 
will continue to gradually strength through today as it pushes 
eastward. Shortwave energy out ahead of the trough will push across 
the Florida peninsula this afternoon and overnight. At the surface, 
high pressure across the Great Lakes region will remain in place, as 
a weakening boundary stalls across north Florida. An area of low 
pressure is forecast to develop across the southeastern Gulf near 
Cuba tonight. Locally, moisture will increase this afternoon and 
overnight in the northeasterly flow. Forecast PW values this 
afternoon are 1.3-1.7" before increasing to 1.7-1.9" tonight. This 
increase in moisture will also result in increasing cloud cover in 
the mid and upper levels. The passing energy aloft has provided 
enough support for the development of isolated showers this 
afternoon, mainly along the Treasure Coast and out in the Atlantic 
waters. Otherwise, mostly dry conditions are forecast tonight. As 
moisture continues to increase tonight, rain chances will also begin 
to increase, with a low to medium (20-40%) chance of rain near and 
north of the I-4 corridor, and a medium to high (50-60%) chance of 
rain southward. At this time, lightning storm chances (20%) remain 
confined to over the local Atlantic waters tonight. 

The Weather Prediction Center (WPC) maintains portions of east 
central Florida in a Marginal Risk (level 1 out of 4) of excessive
rainfall starting tonight, for Brevard, Okeechobee, and the 
Treasure Coast counties. A Flood Watch will begin at 1 AM across 
these areas tonight due to the ongoing sensitivities from prior 
rainfall events. Temperatures will be seasonable today, with 
afternoon highs in the low to mid 70s. Overnight lows will fall 
into the low to mid 60s across the north, and mid to upper 60s 
across the south. 

Wednesday-Thursday... An upper level trough over the central US on 
Wednesday will shift eastward through the period, becoming further 
enhanced by a closed low shifting southward across the midwest, 
which will help the trough deepen over the southeastern US Wednesday 
into Thursday. The trough axis is forecast to shift eastward over 
the Florida peninsula early Thursday before lifting northeast 
through the day. At the surface, a low pressure system near the 
Keys/ South Florida on Wednesday will lift northeastward across 
South Florida, passing near east central Florida before quickly 
pulling farther northeast and away from Florida on Thursday, aided 
by the aforementioned trough axis over Florida. This will result in 
rain chances increasing through Wednesday as the low lifts 
northeastward. There is a medium to high (40-80%) chance for rain on 
Wednesday, with the highest chances focused primarily across the 
Treasure Coast. Rain chances will begin to decrease into Thursday, 
with some lingering shower activity being possible through the 
morning and early afternoon hours given the trough axis aloft. 
Because of this, have maintained a low (20%) chance of rain on 
Thanksgiving Day (Thursday). Conditions will then trend drier 
through the remainder of Thursday into the overnight hours. 

The Weather Prediction Center (WPC) has outlooked portions of east 
central Florida in a Marginal Risk (level 1 out of 4) of excessive 
rainfall once again on Wednesday, mainly across the Treasure Coast 
counties, Brevard County, and eastern portions of Okeechobee and 
Orange counties. A Flood Watch will remain in effect the Treasure 
Coast, Brevard, and Okeechobee counties through 1 AM Thursday. 
Guidance and ensembles continue to favor rainfall totals around 1-2" 
in these areas, with areas farther north forecast to receive closer 
to 0.5-1". There remains a 10% chance of seeing totals across the 
south closer to 3-4", but confidence in this remains low at this 
time. Regardless of rainfall totals, any rainfall across areas that 
are fully saturated across east central Florida will likely result 
in additional or worsening flooding, with the greatest concern for 
this being primarily focused across coastal communities and those 
along the St. Johns River. While lightning storm activity will be 
limited, there remains a low (20%) chance of lightning storms on 
Wednesday, mainly from Melbourne to Lake Okeechobee south and 
eastward. Guidance is beginning to show a low (20%) chance of 
lightning storms being possible Wednesday night, but have not 
included that into the forecast at this time.  The main storm 
threats at this time will be occasional lightning strikes, wind 
gusts up to 50 mph, and locally heavy rainfall. However, it is 
important to note that if daytime heating occurs, the risk for 
stronger to even severe storms will increase, especially across 
areas south of Melbourne to Kissimmee. At this time, confidence 
remains to low to include strong to severe storm development in 
forecast.However, trends will continue to be closely monitored.

Out
